Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

vignette: John, a 52-year-old North American male and school principal, has been experiencing significant distress following an assault that occurred six months ago. The traumatic event involved an unexpected confrontation with an intruder at his school who brandished a weapon during the afternoon rush. John managed to escape but was left shaken by the experience. Since then, he often finds himself on edge, feeling jumpy and easily startled. This startle response is particularly noticeable in environments where he least expects it, such as during meetings with parents or teachers at his school. Every sound—the slam of a locker door, the sudden closing of a classroom window—can trigger an immediate fight-or-flight reaction within him. John’s scanning behavior has become a habitual part of his daily routine. As soon as he enters any room or building, whether it's the school cafeteria for lunch or the faculty lounge during a break, he instinctively looks around to identify all possible exits. This constant vigilance helps him feel slightly more in control but also leaves him feeling perpetually tense and anxious. Interestingly, John notices potential weapons or dangerous objects in his surroundings almost subconsciously. During one staff meeting, he found himself fixating on the small paperweights on each desk, imagining how they could be used as projectiles or blunt instruments. This hyper-awareness of danger has become a constant shadow over his interactions and activities. The memory of the assault is another source of significant distress for John. When he tries to deliberately recall the details of what happened, the memories are fragmented and difficult to access. However, these memories tend to replay involuntarily in vivid detail, like scenes from a film that loop endlessly in his mind. For instance, while driving home from work or lying awake at night, John finds himself reliving those few terrifying moments with alarming clarity. What frightens him most is the physical reenactment of these memories. When he thinks about the event, his body involuntarily mimics the positions and sensations he experienced during the assault—his heart rate increases, his muscles tense up, and he feels a surge of adrenaline as if he were right back in that moment. This bodily reenactment is especially distressing because it reinforces his sense of vulnerability and danger. John’s wife has noticed these changes in him over time. He used to be calm and composed, leading the school with confidence. Now, she sees how the assault has left him feeling on high alert, always scanning for threats and reacting sharply to sudden movements or loud noises. His constant state of hypervigilance has started to affect his relationships as well; he often avoids social gatherings where he might feel exposed or unsafe. Recently, John has become increasingly aware that these symptoms are impacting not only his personal life but also his professional responsibilities. He finds it challenging to focus on administrative tasks and is frequently distracted by intrusive thoughts about the assault. This preoccupation with safety has led him to become overly cautious in his interactions with students and staff, which can be perceived as aloof or distant. What finally brought John to seek help was a particularly distressing episode at work where he overreacted during an emergency drill, assuming it was another threat rather than a routine exercise. The incident left him feeling embarrassed and frustrated with himself for not being able to control his reactions. He recognizes that something needs to change if he is to regain some sense of normalcy in his life. John is most hoping for strategies to manage these overwhelming feelings of fear and anxiety, particularly the intrusive memories and constant vigilance. He wants to feel more grounded and less on edge so that he can return to leading a fulfilling professional and personal life without being consumed by the traumatic event.
